reader.title: Killing of Hampton Price
bases: Every account has a single officer, Constable or Town Sergeant Oliver, shooting Price while trying to arrest him or collect money from him, with no crowd involved (A1, A3, A6).

Separate Norfolk dispatches agree that an officer named Oliver fatally shot a Black man named Price at Franklin, Va. (A1, A3, A6), though they disagree on the day, Price's calling, the cause of the quarrel and how he was shot.

summary.text: The killing of Hampton Price was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable Thomas Oliver at Franklin, in Southampton County, Virginia, in December 1881.
Price died of the wound, and the only accounts, all given from the officer's side, said Price had struck Oliver with a heavy object before he fired.
The shooting reached papers from Virginia to Maine and Nebraska in two conflicting versions, one describing Price as a preacher on a spree and the other as a conjuror shot in the back while fleeing.
The first reports called Price "a colored preacher" of Southampton County, and the Daily Gazette headlined its item "The Parson's Last Spree."
A later Norfolk dispatch instead described him as "a negro conjurer and so-called doctor" who had come to Franklin after falling on hard times in his own neighborhood.
In that version an elderly Black man paid Price fifty cents for a charm meant to lead him to a mine of gold coins and then demanded the money back when it failed.
According to Norfolk dispatches dated December 15, Price was shot on Monday night, December 12, by Constable Thomas Oliver, known as Tom.
The National Republican said Price had been in a fight and knocked the constable down with "a heavy missile" when approached, after which "the officer then shot him."
The Daily Gazette said Price resisted arrest by knocking the constable down with a "black jack," and that the constable fired at Price as he lay on the ground, wounding him in the abdomen.
Price died on the night of Wednesday, December 14.

The conjuror version held that Town Sergeant Oliver went to Price to renew the old man's demand for his money, and that Price refused and struck him four or five blows over the head with a black-jack.
Oliver then drew his pistol and shot Price in the back as he ran.
No report of an inquest, an arrest of the officer or any legal proceeding appears in the coverage.

News of the shooting first appeared as a single sentence in the Richmond Dispatch, which called the victim "the negro Price," and as a two-sentence item among the National Republican's "Virginia News."
The National Republican and the Gazette both repeated the officer's account of being attacked, with the Gazette's headline mocking the dead man as a parson on a spree.
The conjuror story, as printed in the Washington Evening Star on December 19, treated the case as a curiosity "under peculiar circumstances."
The Delaware Daily Republican's fuller version said Price had come to try "his conjuring scheme on the ignorant negroes there" and recounted the shot in the back without comment.

The same story ran in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer that day, as a one-line item in the Daily Kennebec Journal on December 21, and in the Omaha Daily Bee, credited to the Star, on January 2, 1882.
The two versions differ on the date, giving Monday night in the December 15 dispatches and Friday night in the conjuror story.
The Monday date is better supported, since the Richmond Dispatch had already reported Price dead on December 16, before the Friday on which the later story placed the shooting.
The accounts also disagree on Oliver's title, on whether Price was resisting arrest or refusing to repay money, and on whether he was shot lying on the ground or in the back while fleeing.

accounts.label: Norfolk dispatches of Dec. 15 (arrest version)
accounts.gist: Price, a colored preacher, was fighting or 'on a spree' on Monday night, resisted arrest by knocking Constable Oliver down with a heavy object or 'black jack,' and was shot, dying Wednesday night; one version says the constable fired as Price lay on the ground.

accounts.label: Norfolk dispatch (conjuror version)
accounts.gist: Hampton Price, a conjuror, refused to return fifty cents taken for a gold-finding charm, struck Town Sergeant Oliver several blows with a black-jack when he demanded it, and was shot in the back as he fled.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch and National Republican ran one- or two-sentence items among other state news, the Dispatch calling him 'the negro Price.'
The Daily Gazette headlined it 'The Parson's Last Spree' and gave the resisting-arrest version, while reporting that the constable fired at Price on the ground.
The conjuror version cast Price as a swindler of 'the ignorant negroes' and described the shooting as following his assault on the officer, without comment on his being shot in the back.
The conjuror story ran as a curiosity in Pennsylvania, Maine and Nebraska papers into January 1882.

versions.value: Shot Monday night (Dec. 12), died Wednesday night (Dec. 14)

conflicts.note: The Monday date is better supported: the Richmond Dispatch telegram of Dec. 15 already reported Price dead, before the Friday given later.
Only the later accounts give the first name Hampton.
